source_org: Social Security Administration Office of the Chief Actuary
source_title: Letters on the SSI Savings Penalty Elimination Act (2026) and the SSI Restoration Act (2021)
design_differences: Platform arithmetic built from published estimates. Asset limits ($10,000/$20,000, indexed): $8.9B over 2025-2034, effective 2027. Income exclusions restored to about $128 and $416 a month, indexed: $60B over 2021-2030. High end adjusts for the later budget window. Sum ignores interactions.

program: SNAP changes including reversal of 2025 cuts

source_title: R48552, SNAP and Related Nutrition Programs in P.L. 119-21
design_differences: Cost of reversal taken as CBO's $187B estimate of the 2025 nutrition cuts. Understates cost: excludes the platform's broader disability exemption and verification grace period, and actual 2026 SNAP spending fell further than CBO projected.

source_title: JCT estimate of permanent 2021 expansion (via CRS IN11823); TPC, Congress Could Again Help Low-Income Workers
design_differences: Same design as the platform (2021 expansion made permanent: about three times the credit, eligibility from age 19). Final parameters are set after scoring (Section 4.3).

source_title: Make the Child Tax Credit Fully Refundable
design_differences: Same design as the platform: the $2,200 credit made fully refundable with no earnings requirement. $272B conventional, $335B dynamic.

program: Child Tax Credit: young child supplement
source_title: The Potential Cost of New Entitlements
design_differences: Platform arithmetic: $1,000 per child under age 6, fully refundable and indexed, scaled from Concord Coalition's $44B a year for a $1,000 credit for all children under 17 to the under-6 share and inflation. Low confidence.

Set by the statutory cap in Section 3.6.9: $5B a year, indexed for inflation (about $55B over ten years). For scale, FY2026 funding is about $1.1B for WIOA dislocated-worker grants, $0.3B for apprenticeship grants, and $0.05B for Trade Adjustment Assistance.
Not yet estimated; the existing credit is small, and the expansion's size depends on parameters not yet set.

program: Housing vouchers for people experiencing or at risk of homelessness
source_org: National Alliance to End Homelessness (platform arithmetic)
source_title: How Much Would It Cost to Provide Housing First to All Households Staying in Homeless Shelters?
design_differences: Platform arithmetic. Low end: NAEH's $9.6B a year in added funding to house every household in shelter, times ten. High end roughly doubles it for unsheltered households and those at imminent risk (McKinney-Vento), which NAEH excludes. NAEH prices a mix of rapid re-housing and supportive housing, not vouchers alone. Vouchers last while a household stays eligible, so later years may cost more. Low confidence.

program: Emergency rental assistance and right to counsel
source_org: Legal Services Corporation; Ellen and O'Regan (Aspen Economic Strategy Group) (platform arithmetic)
source_title: LSC estimate of representation in all eviction cases; Ellen, Ganz and O'Regan, temporary rental assistance proposal
design_differences: Platform arithmetic. Right to counsel: LSC's $3.3B to $4.1B a year for all eviction cases, phased in over five years (about 8 full years of cost in the window): $26B to $33B. Overstates slightly, since the platform covers tenants under 200% of poverty, not all tenants. Rental assistance: Ellen and O'Regan's about $4.5B a year base program: $45B. Excludes the capped recession increase, which is paid only when the Section 1.2 trigger is met. Medium-low confidence.

High end adds back the 40% of children CBO assumed live in states that would not take part, since the platform guarantees access nationwide. Older budget window likely understates current costs. Low confidence.

Not yet estimable: the cap depends on the long-term care benefit in Section 5.1, which is still an open question (Section 5.1.7). For scale only: the Urban Institute (2020) estimated added federal spending of $355B to $526B over ten years for options that add long-term services and supports to a public health plan. Not used in the affordability test.

source_title: 10 Education Priorities America Could Afford If Everyone Paid All Their Taxes
design_differences: Platform arithmetic using one reference design: tripling Title I, an added $36B a year on 2023 funding, times ten, with the high end allowing for growth. Section 7.2.1 sets no dollar amount; resources 'substantially equivalent' to wealthier districts could cost more. Low confidence.

source_org: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget; Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce
source_title: Elizabeth Warren's Higher Education Plan (update of CRFB's estimate of the College for All Act); The Dollars and Sense of Free College
design_differences: Low end: CRFB's updated cost of the College for All Act (about $700B), in which the federal government pays 67% and states the rest. High end: Georgetown's $800B total cost of a universal first-dollar tuition program over 11 years. The platform covers tuition at all public institutions for all students and does not yet set a federal-state split; if the federal government paid the full cost, the high end applies. Redirecting existing aid to living costs (Section 7.3) is not counted as savings. Medium-low confidence.

source_title: Cost estimate for S. 2432 (2014); letter on income-driven repayment (2023)
design_differences: Not yet estimable. Refinancing every federal loan at 0.01%, discharge after 240 qualifying payments, and an end to capitalized interest go far beyond any scored proposal. For scale only: CBO scored a 2014 bill refinancing about half of federal loans at about 4% at $51B over ten years, and the 2023 income-driven repayment rule at about $230B to $276B. The platform's version would very likely cost several hundred billion dollars. Section 7.3.1 requires a published estimate before implementation.
